questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Expression for the Domain of a Transformed Tangent or Cotangent Function
questions.problem: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The domain of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ is given by

$$
x\ne n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $2\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+1,$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).$ This gives

$$
x-\frac{\pi }{4}\ne n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{4} & \ne n\pi  \\ x & \ne n\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi ,$ where $n$ is an integer.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Expression for the Zeros of a Transformed Tangent or Cotangent Function
questions.problem: Which of the following expressions gives all of the zeros of the function $f(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The zeros of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ are given by

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the zeros of $f(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(x-\frac{\pi }{3}).$ This gives

$$
x-\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-\frac{\pi }{3} & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi +\frac{\pi }{3} \\ x & =\frac{5\pi }{6}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the zeros are $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}+n\pi ,$ where $n$ is an integer.

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, we conclude that the zeros are $x=\frac{5\pi }{6}+n\pi ,$ where $n$ is an integer.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Expression for the Asymptotes of a Transformed Tangent or Cotangent Function
questions.problem: Which of the following expressions gives all of the vertical asymptotes of the function  $f(x)=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The asymptotes of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ are given by the expression

$$
x=n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the asymptotes of $\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(2x-\frac{\pi }{4}).$ This gives

$$
2x-\frac{\pi }{4}=n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =n\pi  \\ 2x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{n\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the expression giving all the vertical asymptotes is $x=\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{n\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.

questions.problem:
Which of the following expressions gives all of the vertical asymptotes of the function  $f(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)-5,$  where 
$x$ is measured in degrees? Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The asymptotes of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ are given by the expression

$$
x=n\cdot {180}^{∘},
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the asymptotes of $2\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)-5,$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(3x).$ This gives

$$
3x=n\cdot {180}^{∘}.
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ x & =\frac{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}{3} \\ x & =n\cdot {60}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the expression giving all the vertical asymptotes is $x=n\cdot {60}^{∘},$ where $n$ is an integer.

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, we conclude that the expression giving all the vertical asymptotes is $x=n\cdot {60}^{∘},$ where $n$ is an integer.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a General Expression for the Domain of a Transformed Tangent or Cotangent Function
questions.problem: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(4x+\frac{\pi }{6})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The domain of $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is given by the expression

$$
x\ne \frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $\operatorname{tan}⁡(4x+\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(4x+\frac{\pi }{6}).$ This gives

$$
4x+\frac{\pi }{6}\ne \frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+\frac{\pi }{6} & \ne \frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi  \\ 4x & \ne \frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi -\frac{\pi }{6} \\ 4x & \ne \frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi  \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{3\cdot 4}+\frac{n\pi }{4} \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne \frac{\pi }{12}+\frac{n\pi }{4},$ where $n$ is an integer.
